facts.statement: Hylaeosaurus was one of the first dinosaurs discovered, found in 1832 by Gideon Mantell.
facts.quote: Hylaeosaurus was one of the first dinosaurs to be discovered, in 1832 by Gideon Mantell.

facts.statement: Hylaeosaurus fossils were found in the Grinstead Clay.
facts.quote: It was found in the Grinstead Clay.

facts.statement: Hylaeosaurus was about five meters long.
facts.quote: Hylaeosaurus was about five metres long.

facts.statement: On July 20, 1832, Gideon Mantell reported finding saurian bones in boulders freed by a gunpowder explosion at a quarry in Tilgate Forest.
facts.quote: On 20 July 1832, fossil collector Gideon Mantell wrote to Professor Benjamin Silliman that when a gunpowder explosion had demolished a quarry rock face in Tilgate Forest, several of the boulders freed showed the bones of a saurian.

facts.statement: In November 1832, Mantell decided to create the new generic name Hylaeosaurus.
facts.quote: In November 1832 Mantell decided to create a new generic name: Hylaeosaurus.

facts.statement: On December 19, Mantell chose the specific name armatus, meaning 'armed' or 'armoured', referring to the spikes and armor plates.
facts.quote: Mantell on 19 December chose armatus, Latin for "armed" or "armoured", in reference to the spikes and armour plates.

facts.statement: Hylaeosaurus armatus was validly named in May 1833 when Mantell published The Geology of the South-East of England.
facts.quote: In May 1833 his The Geology of the South-East of England appeared, hereby validly naming the type species Hylaeosaurus armatus.

facts.statement: Hylaeosaurus was one of the three animals used by Richard Owen to define the group Dinosauria in 1842, alongside Megalosaurus and Iguanodon.
facts.quote: Hylaeosaurus is the most obscure of the three animals used by Sir Richard Owen to first define the new group Dinosauria, in 1842, the other genera being Megalosaurus and Iguanodon.

facts.statement: The original Hylaeosaurus specimen recovered by Mantell from Tilgate Forest was acquired by the Natural History Museum of London in 1838.
facts.quote: The original specimen, recovered by Gideon Mantell from the Tilgate Forest, was in 1838 acquired by the Natural History Museum of London.

facts.statement: The stone block containing the holotype measures about 135 by 75 centimeters.
facts.quote: The block measures about 135 by 75 centimetres.

facts.statement: Limited information from preparations by Mark Graham since 2003 was published in 2020 along with a revised description.
facts.quote: The limited information gained by the preparations by Mark Graham since 2003, was published in 2020, together with a revised description.

facts.statement: Additional remains have been referred to Hylaeosaurus from the Isle of Wight, France, Germany, Spain, and Romania.
facts.quote: Additional remains have been referred to Hylaeosaurus, from the Isle of Wight, (the Ardennes of) France, Bückeberg Formation, Germany, Spain and Romania.

facts.statement: In 1840, Owen hypothesized that the asymmetrical spikes were not on the back but were incorrectly assumed to be gastralia or belly-ribs.
facts.quote: Owen in 1840 developed a new hypothesis about the spikes; noting they were asymmetrical he correctly rejected the notion they formed a row on the back but incorrectly assumed they were gastralia or belly-ribs.

facts.statement: Mantell suggested that Hylaeosaurus either had a row of spines on its back forming a dermal fringe or possessed the same appendage on its tail.
facts.quote: As Mantell himself put it: "there appears every reason to conclude that either its back was armed with a formidable row of spines, constituting a dermal fringe, or that its tail possessed the same appendage".

facts.statement: It is debated whether Polacanthus is the same species as Hylaeosaurus armatus, despite differences in their osteology.
facts.quote: It has also been suggested that Polacanthus is simply the same species as Hylaeosaurus armatus and thus a junior synonym, but there are a number of differences in their osteology.

facts.statement: Gideon Mantell originally estimated that Hylaeosaurus was about 7.6 meters long.
facts.quote: Gideon Mantell originally estimated that Hylaeosaurus was about 7.6 m long, or about half the size of the other two original dinosaurs, Iguanodon and Megalosaurus.

facts.statement: Mantell originally modeled Hylaeosaurus after a modern lizard.
facts.quote: At the time, he modelled the animal after a modern lizard.

facts.statement: Modern estimates of Hylaeosaurus length range up to 6 meters.
facts.quote: Modern estimates range up to 6 m in length.

facts.statement: Gregory S. Paul estimated in 2010 that Hylaeosaurus was 5 meters long and weighed 2 tonnes.
facts.quote: Gregory S. Paul in 2010 estimated the length at 5 m, the weight at 2 tonne.

facts.statement: In 2001, Darren Naish and colleagues estimated the length of Hylaeosaurus at 3 to 4 meters.
facts.quote: Some estimates are considerably lower: in 2001 Darren Naish e.a. gave a length of 3-4 m.

facts.statement: Maidment identified two unique traits of Hylaeosaurus: an unfused scapula and coracoid and three long shoulder spines.
facts.quote: Maidment gave two autapomorphies, unique derived traits: the scapula did not fuse with the coracoid, even when the animal was of a considerable size; there were three long spines on its shoulder.

facts.statement: Hylaeosaurus is described as having rows of armor plating on its back and tail, a long head, and a beak for cropping low vegetation.
facts.quote: Hylaeosaurus is often styled as a fairly typical nodosaur, with rows of armour plating on the back and tail combined with a relatively long head, equipped with a beak used to crop low-lying vegetation.

facts.statement: Kenneth Carpenter described the skull and lower jaw remains of Hylaeosaurus in 2001.
facts.quote: In 2001 the skull and lower jaws remains were described by Kenneth Carpenter.

facts.statement: Hylaeosaurus possessed a triangular postorbital horn.
facts.quote: A triangular postorbital horn was present.

facts.statement: The shoulder blade of Hylaeosaurus features a sharp 120-degree angle between the acromion and the proximal plate.
facts.quote: On the shoulder blade, there is a sharp angle of 120° between the acromion and the proximal plate.

facts.statement: The front shoulder spine of Hylaeosaurus is the longest, measuring 42.5 centimeters.
facts.quote: The front spine is the longest at 42.5 centimetres

facts.statement: A fourth forward-pointing spine is located immediately behind the skull of Hylaeosaurus.
facts.quote: A fourth spine, of about the same build but more forward-pointing, is present immediately behind the skull.

facts.statement: In 2013, Sven Sachs and Jahn Hornung suggested a configuration of five lateral neck spines for Hylaeosaurus.
facts.quote: In 2013 Sven Sachs and Jahn Hornung suggested a configuration in which there were five lateral neck spines, the new German spine having a morphology adapted to fit in the third position.

facts.statement: Gideon Mantell discovered Hylaeosaurus in 1832.
facts.quote: Hylaeosaurus fue uno de los primeros dinosaurios descubiertos en 1832 por Gideon Mantell.

facts.statement: Richard Owen based the classification of Dinosauria on Hylaeosaurus in 1842.
facts.quote: En 1842 fue uno de los tres dinosaurios en los que Richard Owen basó el Dinosauria.

facts.statement: Only the species Hylaeosaurus armatus is currently considered valid within the genus Hylaeosaurus.
facts.quote: Cuatro especies fueron nombradas en el género, pero solo la especie tipo Hylaeosaurus armatus se considera actualmente válida.

facts.statement: Coombs assigned Hylaeosaurus to the family Nodosauridae in 1978.
facts.quote: In 1978 Coombs assigned it to the Nodosauridae within the Ankylosauria.

facts.statement: In the 1990s, some researchers mistakenly classified polacanthines like Hylaeosaurus as basal ankylosaurids due to a belief they had small tail clubs.
facts.quote: However, in the 1990s, the polacanthines were sometimes seen as basal ankylosaurids, because they were mistakenly believed to have small tail-clubs.

facts.statement: A popular modern classification places Hylaeosaurus in Polacanthidae, a basal group outside the nodosaurid and ankylosaurid clades.
facts.quote: A more popular alternative today is that they formed a Polacanthidae, a basal group outside of the nodosaurids + ankylosaurids clade.

facts.statement: The genus Hylaeosaurus was named by Mantell in 1833.
facts.quote: genus_authority: Mantell, 1833

facts.statement: The species Hylaeosaurus armatus was named by Mantell in 1833.
facts.quote: species_authority: Mantell, 1833

facts.statement: Only limited remains of Hylaeosaurus have been found, leaving much of its anatomy unknown.
facts.quote: Solo se han encontrado restos limitados de Hylaeosaurus y gran parte de su anatomía es desconocida.

facts.statement: It is debated whether Hylaeosaurus was a basal nodosaurid or a basal ankylosaurian.
facts.quote: Podría haber sido un nodosáurido basal, aunque un análisis cladístico reciente lo recupera como un anquilosauriano basal.

facts.statement: The damaged and shifted skull elements of Hylaeosaurus provided little useful information.
facts.quote: The damaged and shifted skull elements provided little information.

facts.statement: Fósiles de Hylaeosaurus fueron descubiertos en el Bosque de Tilgate tras una explosión de pólvora en una cantera en julio de 1832.
facts.quote: El 20 de julio de 1832, el coleccionista de fósiles Gideon Mantell le escribió al profesor Benjamin Silliman que cuando una explosión de pólvora demolió una roca de cantera en el Bosque de Tilgate, varias de las rocas liberadas mostraron los huesos de un sauriano.

facts.statement: El esqueleto de Hylaeosaurus fue el dinosaurio no aviar más completo conocido hasta la fecha de su descubrimiento.
facts.quote: De hecho, el descubrimiento representó el esqueleto de dinosaurio no aviar más completo que se conocía en ese momento.

facts.statement: El nombre Hylaeosaurus significa "lagarto de bosque" y fue elegido en referencia al Bosque de Tilgate donde se encontró.
facts.quote: Mantell originalmente reclamó el nombre de Hylaeosaurus que significa "lagarto de bosque", por el Bosque de Tilgate en el que fue descubierto.

facts.statement: Mantell posteriormente interpretó el nombre como "lagarto de Wealden", refiriéndose al Grupo Wealden, la formación geológica del Cretácico temprano donde se halló.
facts.quote: Más tarde, afirmó que significaba " lagarto de Wealden", "wealden" es otra palabra para bosque, en referencia al Grupo Wealden, el nombre de la formación geológica del Cretácico temprano en la que se encontró por primera vez al dinosaurio.

facts.statement: El holotipo de Hylaeosaurus, recuperado por Gideon Mantell, se encuentra ahora en el Museo de Historia Natural de Londres con el número de inventario NHMUK 3775.
facts.quote: El espécimen original, recuperado por Gideon Mantell del Bosque de Tilgate , fue posteriormente adquirido por el Museo de Historia Natural de Londres. Tiene el número de inventario NHMUK 3775, anteriormente BMNH R3775.

facts.statement: El holotipo de Hylaeosaurus data del Valanginiense, hace aproximadamente 137 millones de años.
facts.quote: Se encontró en una capa de la Formación de Grinstead Clay que data del Valanginiense, de unos 137 millones de años.

facts.statement: El bloque de piedra que contiene el holotipo de Hylaeosaurus mide aproximadamente 135 por 75 centímetros.
facts.quote: El bloque mide unos 135 por 75 centímetros.

facts.statement: Varios hallazgos de la Bretaña continental han sido atribuidos a Hylaeosaurus armatus.
facts.quote: Varios hallazgos de la parte continental Bretaña han sido referidos a Hylaeosaurus armatus.

facts.statement: En 2011, Paul Barrett y Susannah Maidment concluyeron que solo el holotipo puede asociarse con certeza a Hylaeosaurus armatus debido a la presencia de Polacanthus en las mismas capas.
facts.quote: Sin embargo, en 2011, Paul Barrett y Susannah Maidment concluyeron que solo el holotipo podía asociarse con certeza a la especie, en vista de la presencia de Polacanthus en las mismas capas.

facts.statement: Restos adicionales han sido referidos a Hylaeosaurus desde la Isla de Wight, las Ardenas de Francia, Alemania, España y Rumania.
facts.quote: Se han remitido restos adicionales a Hylaeosaurus , de la Isla de Wight, las Ardenas de Francia, Alemania, España y Rumania.

facts.statement: Hylaeosaurus armatus es actualmente la única especie válida reconocida en el género.
facts.quote: Hylaeosaurus armatus Mantell 1833 se considera actualmente la única especie válida en el género.

facts.statement: Alfred Romer renombró a Regnosaurus northhamptoni como Hylaeosaurus northhamptoni en 1956.
facts.quote: En 1956, Alfred Romer cambió el nombre de Regnosaurus northhamptoni a Hylaeosaurus northhamptoni.

facts.statement: Walter Coombs renombró a Polacanthus como Hylaeosaurus foxii en 1971.
facts.quote: Polacanthus nombrado por Owen en 1865 fue nombrada por Walter Coombs en 1971 Hylaeosaurus foxii.

facts.statement: Se ha sugerido que Polacanthus es un sinónimo de Hylaeosaurus armatus, aunque existen diferencias osteológicas significativas.
facts.quote: También se ha sugerido que Polacanthus es simplemente la misma especie que Hylaeosaurus armatus y por lo tanto un sinónimo más moderno, pero hay una serie de diferencias en su osteología.

facts.statement: Hylaeosaurus fue el primer anquilosauriano descubierto, pero sus afinidades taxonómicas permanecieron inciertas durante mucho tiempo.
facts.quote: Hylaeosaurus fue el primer anquilosauriano descubierto, pero hasta bien entrado el , sus afinidades exactas seguirían siendo inciertas.

facts.statement: En 1978, Walter Coombs clasificó a Hylaeosaurus dentro de la familia Nodosauridae.
facts.quote: En 1978, Coombs lo asignó a los Nodosauridae dentro de la Ankylosauria.

facts.statement: Una clasificación popular actual sitúa a Hylaeosaurus en la familia Polacanthidae, un grupo basal fuera de los nodosáuridos y anquilosáuridos.
facts.quote: Una alternativa más popular hoy en día es que formaron un familia, Polacanthidae, un grupo basal fuera del clado de los nodosáuridos y anquilosáuridos.

facts.statement: Hylaeosaurus vivió desde el Berriasiense hasta el Albiano, entre 139.1 y 110.1 millones de años atrás.
facts.quote: Time range: Berriasian to Albian (139.1 to 110.1 million years ago)

facts.statement: El grupo parental de Hylaeosaurus es la familia Nodosauridae.
facts.quote: Parent group: Nodosauridae

facts.statement: Hylaeosaurus pertenece a la familia Nodosauridae.

facts.statement: Hylaeosaurus se clasifica dentro de la clase Ornithischia.
facts.quote: Class: Ornithischia
